newsitem.title: UK: Coffee futures soar, physical differentials mixed.
newsitem.headline: Coffee futures soar, physical differentials mixed.

text.p: Robusta coffee futures soared by nearly 16 percent to $1,550 a tonne in the week but robusta differentials headed south on pressure from African supplies.
But arabica premiums continued to hold steady on the back of a Colombia dock workers strike, expectations of lower Brazilian crop and news of lower supplies from other central American origins.
"Prices are going through the roof," said one trader.
Another said, "Everybody is now bullish... roasters need coffee but they prefer to wait to fix prices. We will see large roaster support if prices fall by eight to nine cents (a lb)."
The first trader noted that large coffee manufacturers were pretty well covered until July.
"They just need to fix some of their prices but are unwilling to now with prices rising."

London's surging futures prices took another sharp upward move on Wednesday on renewed New York strength following news Colombian exports in January might be 300,000 bags less than anticipated if a continuing strike at the port of Buenaventura continued.
Early Wednesday talks aimed at ending a week-old dockworkers' strike in the Pacific port ended in a deadlock. The port ships about 60 percent of Colombia's coffee exports and all its sugar exports.

Besides the Brazilian crop forecasts, there were also news of a posibble drop in harvest or exports from Mexico, Honduras and Nicaragua, which along with Brazil and Colombia are major arabica growers.

Earlier in the week, London gained support from news Vietnam might join a producer group now meeting in Rio de Janeiro to consider proposals for further cut in members exports for the first half of 1997.
Traders said cash differentials for robusta coffee, grown mainly in Africa and Asia, were weighed by growing supplies from Cameroon and Ivory Coast.
"There are plenty of offers from Cameroon and Ivory Coast. Cameroon was late to offer coffee until two weeks ago as it was occupied with cocoa sales," said one Swiss trader.
In differentials, Colombian Excelso (screen 15) was quoted at 15 cents over New York FOB while Guatemalan strictly hard beans (new crop) was quoted 7.50 cents over New York.

Cameroon grade one was quoted at $15-$20 over London CIF Europe, down from $60 two weeks ago while Ivory Coast grade two was quoted at $30 below London, against at par a forthnight ago. -- London newsroom +44 171 542 4985
